thread.title: Big Tech: You Want the Good News or the Bad News?

title: Big Tech: You Want the Good News or the Bad News?
text:
Jon Swartz June 30, 2018
Excuse technology investors if they’re showing signs of severe whiplash. Such are the consequences of a week in which they were wrenched by geopolitical and high court decisions that pained and soothed.
The week got off to a troubling start on Monday, when shares of Apple (AAPL), Qualcomm (QCOM), IBM (IBM), and other tech stalwarts were battered by reports of new Trump administration plans to target China’s involvement with U.S. technology.
After managing to skirt the tariff debate, the news suddenly had Silicon Valley in the crosshairs of a potential trade war. The Nasdaq Composite Index dropped 2.1% on Monday, its worst day in nearly three months.
If implemented, the initiatives would limit China’s ability to invest in the U.S. tech sector and block additional technology exports to Beijing. Exports of U.S.-produced technology judged crucial to national security, ranging from robotics to cryptography, would most likely face restrictions.
It didn’t take long for the White House to backtrack from the most worrisome plans. By Tuesday, President Donald Trump, in a less-confrontational approach, said he could rely on an existing U.S. committee to scrutinize foreign acquisitions for national security risks. On Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin tried to make China seem like less of a target in the latest actions. But the damage was done. The Nasdaq finished the week down 2.4%, its worst percentage decline since the week ending March 23.
Qualcomm shares could be among the first casualties of the China tensions. Its proposed $44 billion acquisition of Dutch firm NXP Semiconductors (NXPI) still awaits approval in China, where Qualcomm is one of the most prominent and successful U.S. companies. Nearly two-thirds of its annual revenue ($14.3 billion) came from China in the past 12 months. Among U.S. tech companies, only Apple and Intel (INTC) generate more revenue there, according to FactSet. That puts Qualcomm in an awkward spot with the White House.
Its shares are down 12% so far this year, even with the Nasdaq Composite up 8.7% over the same period. Qualcomm didn’t reply to an email message seeking comment on tariffs.
Then there is Apple. Over the past 12 months, about 18% of its revenue ($45 billion) came from China, where it shipped more than 41 million iPhones. The company has about 40 stores in China, or 8% of its worldwide outlets. But those numbers underestimate China’s importance to Apple. After all, every iPhone, regardless of where it’s sold, is assembled in a Chinese factory.
CEO Tim Cook frequently travels to China, and in April he visited the White House to seek assurances from Trump that iPhones built in China wouldn’t be affected by tariffs. “I talked about trade and the importance of trade, and how I felt that two countries trading together make the pie larger,” Cook said last month of his White House trip, in an interview with Carlyle Group co-founder David Rubenstein. “I felt that tariffs weren’t the right approach there. I showed him some analytical kind of things to demonstrate why.”
When we reached out to Apple, the company had no additional comment on Trump’s latest planned moves in China.
The Information Technology Industry Council, whose members include Apple, Amazon.com (AMZN), and Alphabet (GOOGL), said the administration should “carefully consider the consequences and end goal” of its plan.
“The biggest issue is creating a lot of uncertainty, and uncertainty is never a friend of business,” says Brewer Stone, an expert on China and cross-border mergers who is a partner at boutique investment bank Nfluence Partners.
It isn’t just corporate sales at risk from the potential trade war, but also a huge influx of capital. Investments from the greater China region into U.S. tech companies soared from $2.3 billion in 2014 to $9.9 billion in 2015, while the number of deals jumped from 116 to 188 in the same time frame, according to researcher CB Insights. U.S. tech exports to China amounted to about $30 billion in 2017, out of more than $700 billion in total goods and services. Newsletter Sign-up
While Trump raised one obstacle for tech stocks on Monday, the U.S. Supreme Court minimized another one on Tuesday.
The high court held that American Express (AXP) has a right to stop its partner merchants from offering discounts to consumers using cards from Visa (V) and Mastercard (MA). Those rival cards often carry lower “swipe fees.” AmEx has held on to its market share, despite higher fees, in part by issuing “anti-steering” rules. The Supreme Court declined to see an antitrust violation in that model.
AmEx is more finance than tech, but the ruling could echo throughout Silicon Valley. As tech stocks have rallied, the main risk has been the threat of government intervention. The more powerful that Alphabet, Facebook (FB), and Amazon have gotten, the more some have urged they be broken up. There’s no way to quantify the risk, but surely it has weighed on tech-stock earnings multiples.
However, showing ill effects on complex, multisided markets, as the court seemed to have asked of plaintiffs in the AmEx case, will now be extremely difficult, Stanford Law School professor Douglas Melamed tells Barron’s. The court’s decision, he said, will have considerable influence on how the law develops in growing markets. “This is a court that is hostile to antitrust laws,” Melamed says.
If tech investors lost on Monday, they regained a measure of judicial relief on Tuesday.
